techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

techniques.name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
techniques.description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

resources.title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions
resources.abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

techniques.name: Signal Temporal Logic Monitoring
techniques.description: Signal temporal logic (STL) monitoring checks the signals a system produces over time, such as speeds, distances, positions or a model's outputs, against safety requirements written in signal temporal logic, a formal language for stating how real-valued signals must behave over time intervals (for example, 'whenever the gap to the vehicle ahead falls below 10 m, speed drops below 5 m/s within 2 s'). Each requirement is built from comparisons of signals with thresholds, joined by logical operators and by timed operators such as 'always within [a, b]', 'eventually within [a, b]' and 'until'. For each trace the monitor computes a robustness value, a margin to the requirement rather than robustness to adversarial inputs: its sign says whether the requirement is met (positive) or violated (negative), and its size is a tolerance: any signal whose values stay closer than that to the observed ones at every instant gets the same verdict. Monitors run offline on logged or simulated traces, or online on live signals, where a requirement that looks ahead in time can be decided only once enough of the signal has arrived. RTAMT, the named tool, is an open-source Python library with an optional C++ back-end that builds such monitors from a written specification and connects to ROS and MATLAB/Simulink; its online monitors accept only requirements whose future time windows are bounded and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's time horizon, and it reports the robustness value but does not act on it, so stopping or correcting the system is left to a separate safeguard.

example_use_cases.description: A team developing an adaptive cruise controller with a learned speed policy writes its requirements in STL, for example that the time gap to the vehicle ahead never stays below one second for longer than two seconds, and attaches an RTAMT monitor to every drive in an urban driving simulator. The robustness values show which controller settings meet each requirement and by what margin, and drives with negative values become regression scenarios.

A hospital's service robot, which uses learned perception to find people, fetches supplies along corridors. The integrator monitors live ROS topics against a system requirement (always at least 0.5 m from any detected person) and against one requirement per subsystem, such as the planner reaching its next waypoint in time. When a subsystem requirement fails shortly before the system one, the logged verdicts show where the fault began.

A drone-delivery operator checks each day's flight logs from its learned landing controller against a requirement that, in the last ten seconds before touchdown, descent rate stays below 1 m/s and the drone stays within 0.5 m of the pad centre. It reports the smallest robustness value across all landings to its safety manager and investigates any landing whose value is negative.

limitations.description: The monitor checks the requirement as written, not as intended. Writing correct STL needs fluency in the logic and in the system: a wrong threshold, a time window that is too short or a misplaced operator yields confident positive margins for behaviour the engineers would call unsafe, and nothing in the monitor reveals the mistake. Specifications need the same review as the requirements they encode.

Online monitoring judges a requirement from a partial trace. RTAMT's online monitors take only requirements whose future time windows are bounded, and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's horizon: a check that something happens within five seconds is decided five seconds later, which may be too late to act on in a fast system. Monitors that track a narrowing range of possible robustness values can flag some violations sooner, but stay undecided until the data settles it.

A robustness value is measured in the units of the signals in the requirement, so a margin of 0.4 means 0.4 metres in one requirement and 0.4 degrees in another. Values cannot be compared across requirements, and when one requirement combines signals of different scales its value is set by whichever margin is numerically smallest, which depends on the units chosen unless the signals are normalised first.

Monitoring reports on the traces it sees. A clean record over many hours shows that those runs met the requirement, not that every possible run will, and a violation is reported when it happens, not before, unless a separate predictor of future signals is added. To protect the system, the verdict has to drive a safeguard such as a fallback controller, which the monitor does not provide.

The verdict is only as good as the signals. If a learned perception component misjudges the distance to a person, the monitor computes a confident margin from the wrong distance; independent sensors or ground truth are needed to check the perception itself. Discrete-time monitors see only the samples taken, so a brief violation between samples can go unseen, and the ROS integration assumes messages arrive at a known, regular rate.

techniques.name: SMT-Based Neural Network Verification
techniques.description: SMT-based neural network verification decides exactly whether any input in a defined region can make a trained neural network violate a stated property, and if one can, returns that input as a counterexample. SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers decide whether a set of logical and arithmetic constraints can all hold at once: here the network's weighted sums become linear equations, each piecewise-linear activation such as ReLU becomes a constraint with two cases (inactive at zero, or active and passing its input through), and the input region and the negation of the property become further linear constraints. The solver searches for values that satisfy every constraint with a simplex-based linear-programming engine: it first tries to repair an activation whose current values break it, and splits it into its two cases only when repairs keep failing, while bounds on each neuron (in Marabou, by default, the linear bounds that bound propagation computes) rule cases out early. Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) introduced this lazy treatment of ReLU inside the simplex method and used it on a prototype airborne collision avoidance network; Marabou, its maintained successor, keeps the same search structure with a newer search procedure, adds parallel solving, and can emit a proof certificate for an 'unsatisfiable' answer. The answer is 'unsat', meaning no input in the region violates the property, or 'sat' with a concrete counterexample, and for networks whose activations are all piecewise-linear the procedure is complete; the price is that the number of cases can grow exponentially with the number of neurons, so it is practical for small networks such as controllers, policies and surrogate models with few inputs rather than large image models.

example_use_cases.description: A warehouse robotics team trains hundreds of candidate deep reinforcement learning policies for driving between shelves from range-sensor readings. Before field trials it encodes 'no move into an obstacle in the next step' and 'no repeating left-right loop over several steps' as queries over each small policy network, runs Marabou on every candidate, discards each policy for which a counterexample reading is returned, and takes only the survivors to the physical robot.

An aircraft systems developer replaces a large collision-avoidance lookup table with a set of small neural networks. For each network it writes regions of encounter geometry, such as an intruder close ahead and closing, together with the advisory that must never be issued there, and runs the solver on each. Regions returned as unsatisfiable go into the certification evidence; any counterexample encounter is replayed in simulation and drives retraining.

A medical-device manufacturer uses a small network to recommend infusion rates from a handful of patient measurements. Its safety engineers prove that, for every combination of measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the recommended rate never exceeds the maximum set by the device's hazard analysis, and use any counterexample returned to retrain the network or add an output limit.

limitations.description: Deciding these queries for ReLU networks is NP-complete, and the search may split on every neuron whose case is undecided, so time can grow exponentially with network size and with the number of steps a property spans. In a study of robot navigation policies kept to 16 neurons per hidden layer, single-step collision queries took seconds, but 12-step cycle queries usually ran for hours and nearly three in ten of them hit the 12-hour limit.

The solver runs on ordinary processors, and its own tool paper reports a non-trivial performance gap to GPU-based bound-propagation verifiers, especially on larger networks; in the 2023 verification competition it solved 594 benchmark instances to alpha-beta-CROWN's 721. It is therefore best suited to small networks with few inputs, such as controllers, policies and surrogate models.

Exact answers hold only for piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, max, absolute value and leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh are handled by an over-approximation that is refined step by step, and softmax and bilinear layers only through a convex relaxation, so for networks that use them the procedure is no longer complete and can end without a decisive answer.

The query covers the network and a region of its inputs written as linear constraints, nothing more. A counterexample may lie in a part of the region no real sensor could produce, and a proof says nothing about the environment the network acts in, so choosing a region that is realistic yet small enough to solve takes domain knowledge, and a closed-loop safety claim needs further analysis.

An 'unsat' answer is only as trustworthy as the solver's implementation. Marabou can emit a proof certificate that an independent checker validates, but proof production works with only some of its features and not in parallel mode, and in the tool paper's collision-avoidance experiments certificates were produced for 113 of 180 benchmarks.

techniques.name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
techniques.description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

resources.title: A Kernel Two-Sample Test
resources.abstract: We propose a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which we use to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions.  Our test statistic is the largest difference in expectations over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and is called the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).  We present two distribution-free tests based on large deviation bounds for the MMD, and a third test based on the asymptotic distribution of this statistic.  The MMD can be computed in quadratic time, although efficient linear time approximations are available.  Our statistic is an instance of an integral probability metric, and various classical metrics on distributions are obtained when alternative function classes are used in place of an RKHS.  We apply our two-sample tests  to a variety of problems, including attribute matching for databases using the Hungarian marriage method, where they perform strongly.  Excellent performance is also obtained when comparing distributions over graphs, for which these are the first such tests.

Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
resources.abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

sample_claims.text: Applied to autoencoder representations of 500 images from each source, the kernel two-sample test found no significant difference at the 1 per cent level between the new hospital's chest X-rays and the validation images, and the same test detected the simulated scanner changes that had reduced the model's accuracy in validation.

Every alarm raised by the nightly kernel two-sample test on the fraud model's inputs in the past six months was followed within two working days by an accuracy check on newly labelled cases, and each check either met the accuracy requirement or led to retraining.

In each weekly window since deployment, the loan-application model's production inputs showed no difference from its validation sample detectable by the agreed kernel two-sample test, at a significance level corrected for weekly repetition, and the same test detected the input shifts that had reduced the model's accuracy in pre-deployment trials.
Replayed on reference data alone, the drift monitor's kernel two-sample test raised false alarms at no more than the configured rate of one per quarter.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.

Repeating each reviewed explanation from five random starting masks gives ten highest-weighted edge sets whose pairwise Jaccard index is at least 0.8.

techniques.name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
techniques.description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

example_use_cases.description: Before deploying an open-weights language model as a customer-service assistant, a bank's AI assurance team uses sparse autoencoders published for that model to find features active on prompts where the assistant should refuse to give investment advice. It tests each candidate by suppressing it and measuring the change in refusal rate, and records which labelled features the refusal behaviour depends on in the model's assurance file.

A bioinformatics group using a protein language model to annotate newly sequenced proteins trains sparse autoencoders on its embeddings and compares the features with database annotations of binding sites, structural motifs and domains. Features that match known biology are used to propose candidate annotations for curators to verify, features that fire widely with no clear meaning are flagged for review, and the model's own annotation accuracy is still tested on held-out proteins.

A team that fine-tuned a language model to triage clinical referral letters lists the sparse autoencoder features that most change the 'urgent' score on a validation set, and checks whether they describe clinical content or properties of the letter, such as the referring practice's template. A template feature among the leading drivers is recorded as a finding and leads to retraining on reformatted letters.

limitations.description: The dictionary does not capture everything the layer carries, and what it misses cannot be inspected. In the originating study, replacing one layer of a small language model with its reconstruction raised perplexity from 25 to 40; a concurrent study recovered 79% of a layer's contribution to the loss in its main run. Not finding a feature for a concept does not show that the model lacks it.

The features found are not unique. Larger dictionaries split a feature into narrower ones (one base64 feature at 512 features became three at 4,096), and for a 131,000-feature autoencoder on one layer of Llama 3 8B only about 30% of features were shared by two runs differing only in random seed. A conclusion resting on one feature should name the autoencoder used and be checked on a second run.

Labels are hypotheses drawn from the top-activating examples, and automated scores are modest: the first five features reported in the originating study scored between -0.11 and 0.57, and the advantage over simpler decompositions faded in later layers. Back a label with an intervention that changes the output as the label predicts before citing it as evidence.

It needs the model's internal activations, plus storage and compute to train an autoencoder for each layer studied (one concurrent study trained on 8 billion activation vectors from a single layer). For large models practitioners often rely on autoencoders released for particular open-weights models, so the method is not available for a model reached only through an API.

Being interpretable does not make the features better for a given task. In a 2025 study of detecting concepts from model activations, probes built on autoencoder features did not beat logistic regression on the raw activations on average, and the spurious correlations and data problems they exposed could also be found with simpler baselines. Where detection is the goal, compare against such baselines.

techniques.name: TimeSHAP
techniques.description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

techniques.name: C2PA Content Credentials
techniques.description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

example_use_cases.description: An image-generation service offered in the EU attaches a signed manifest to every image it returns, declaring an AI 'created' action with the service as signer, as its means of meeting the AI Act's Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format. Its compliance team validates a weekly sample of outputs to decide whether marking is working, and registers a watermark soft binding so that a stripped image can be matched back to its record.

A news agency's verification desk runs every image sent in by the public through a C2PA validator before publication. A trusted manifest recording capture on a named camera, with no AI-generated ingredients, lets editors publish it with a provenance label. A manifest naming a generative tool, or a hash that no longer matches, sends it to forensic review, and an image with no credentials is treated as of unknown origin, not as authentic.

An insurer's claims app lets assessors apply an AI tool that enhances and annotates photographs of vehicle damage, and records each AI edit as an action in the photograph's manifest. When a claim is disputed, a reviewing assessor or the claimant's representative can see which changes the AI tool made and check them against the retained original, which the edited photograph's manifest cites as an ingredient.

A social-media platform reads Content Credentials on upload, labels images whose trusted manifest declares a generative AI source, and shows users who signed the record. Its trust-and-safety team tracks what share of uploads carry trusted, untrusted or no credentials, to decide how far its synthetic-media policy can rely on the labels and where it still needs other detection methods.

limitations.description: The record is easy to lose. Anyone can remove the manifest, an attack the C2PA's own threat model expects, and the file is then an ordinary file with no link to its history unless a watermark or fingerprint soft binding was registered with a manifest repository. Because credentials are optional and removable, a file without them says nothing about its origin: the absence of a manifest cannot show that content is human-made or unaltered.

A valid manifest shows who signed the record and that what its hash covers is unchanged, not that its statements are true. A signer can omit an AI step, a stolen key yields manifests that validate, and a camera photographing a screen signs a genuine capture of a staged scene. Validators need not check revocation, metadata such as location may sit outside the hash, and a 2026 preprint found validators disagreeing on the same file, so a result depends on the signer, validator and trust list.

The history is complete only while every tool in the workflow supports C2PA. An edit made in an unsupported tool is not recorded, and if the file later passes through a supporting tool, the new signer implicitly vouches for that unrecorded change, so the chain can show fewer steps than took place. The C2PA itself says the approach depends on widespread adoption by tools and platforms.

Manifests can disclose more than the creator intends, such as capture time and place, device details, the edit history and, through the separate Creator Assertions Working Group identity extension, who made the content. The C2PA's threat model lists identifying creators and tracking viewers as risks. Assertions can be redacted when a file is reused as an ingredient, but people working in risky settings, such as human-rights documentation, must decide what to include before signing.

Support for AI-generated text is immature. Embedding a manifest in plain text, as invisible Unicode characters, entered the specification in version 2.3 and is still marked as under review; the reference SDK supports it only behind an unstable option, and any edit to the text breaks the hash. For language-model output the method is much less dependable than for images, video and audio, where embedding is established.

techniques.name: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Model Inference
techniques.description: A zero-knowledge proof of model inference lets the owner of a model show an outside party that one specific model, fixed in advance, turns a particular input into a particular output, without revealing the model's weights. The owner publishes a commitment to the weights, a short cryptographic fingerprint such as a hash that binds them without disclosing them, together with a verification key that fixes the model's architecture. The model's arithmetic is converted to whole numbers (quantised) and written as a system of equations called a circuit, and for each input a proving system produces a proof, of a few kilobytes to a few hundred kilobytes, that this circuit, run with weights matching the commitment, turns that input into that output; the input can be public or committed in the same way. Anyone holding the verification key can check the proof in milliseconds to seconds: it shows that the committed model gives that output for that input, while keeping the weights hidden, and says nothing about whether that model is accurate, fair or safe. Unlike homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on data it cannot read but gives the caller no evidence of which computation was run, and unlike model signing, which lets someone who holds a model's files check who released them, it lets someone who never sees the weights check individual outputs against them.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-scoring vendor publishes the weight commitment in the report of an independent bias and accuracy audit, which was run on the quantised model bound to that commitment. When a refused applicant complains, the lender's complaints team asks the vendor for a proof for that decision and checks it against the published commitment, to confirm that the audited model gives the same refusal on the applicant's data before it reviews the decision itself.

A hospital trust buying chest X-ray triage results from a cloud provider writes into the contract that its clinical engineering team may challenge a random sample of each month's results. For each sampled case the provider must return a proof against the commitment to the model the trust validated, and the team treats a failed or missing proof as evidence that a different model was served, which triggers the contract's audit clause.

An online-safety regulator inspecting the age-estimation service a platform relies on submits its own test images and asks for a proof with each estimate. Its inspectors check each proof against the commitment registered when an accredited laboratory certified the vendor's model, to decide whether the service in use is the certified model, without the vendor handing its proprietary weights to the regulator.

limitations.description: A valid proof shows that the committed weights turn this input into this output. It does not show that the model is accurate, fair or safe, that the input was genuine, or that the service ran the committed model: a different model giving the same output passes too, so spot checks catch a substituted model only on inputs where the two disagree. A commitment carries assurance only if an audit was run on the model it binds.

Proving costs far more than running the model. Published figures: 88 seconds per prediction of a 15-million-parameter VGG16 on CIFAR-10 images (zkCNN), about 41 minutes for an ImageNet-scale MobileNet on a large cloud server (Kang et al.), and about 13 minutes for one 2,048-token pass of a 13-billion-parameter language model on a data-centre GPU, after a one-off 16-minute commitment (zkLLM). Proving every output of a busy service is impractical, so protocols prove sampled or disputed outputs.

The proof covers a quantised, whole-number version of the model, not the floating-point model that was trained and perhaps audited, and the two can give slightly different outputs. Published attacks plant backdoors that stay dormant at full precision and activate only after quantisation, which EZKL's security notes flag. Audits and accuracy tests must therefore be run on the quantised model that is actually proved, or the commitment and the audit describe different models.

The guarantee depends on configuration. If the weights are private inputs with no published commitment, a proof shows only that some weights for the stated architecture give the output. Hashing the weights inside the proof keeps them hidden but costs about as much again as proving the inference. EZKL's cheaper settings, including its Python default, bind the weights without fully hiding them, and its notes warn they can be recovered from enough proofs. The architecture is normally disclosed.

Soundness rests on the software as well as the mathematics. A compiler error that leaves the equations under-constrained can let a false proof verify, a risk EZKL's documentation names, and EZKL's proofs rely on public parameters from a multi-party set-up ceremony. Audits cover specific releases (EZKL's covered version 21), so verifiers should fix which tool versions and parameters they accept. EZKL, the most used tool, has had no open-source licence since January 2024.
